title: Why it forgets what you told it a while ago
promise: By the end you'll recognize in under a minute that the AI has lost the thread, and you'll know how to move the whole conversation to a new chat with a written handoff, without explaining anything from scratch again.
why: Marta had 140 messages into building the website for her ceramics school. She asked for a color change on the registration button and the AI gave her back code with a pricing section she'd asked to remove two hours earlier, and the button back to blue when they'd been on green all afternoon. She thought she'd broken something, deleted the file, and started from zero: two afternoons in the trash. Nothing was broken. The AI's worktable was full, and the first thing they'd put on it had already fallen off the edge. This lesson is the difference between losing two afternoons and losing two minutes.

theory.title: It doesn't remember: it rereads. And that explains almost everything
theory.text: Every time you hit Enter, you're not talking to the same one that was there a while ago. The app takes the whole conversation from the first message, packs it into an envelope, and sends it back from scratch. It reads it in one pass, writes its answer, and everything gets erased. That stack of pages it rereads every turn is the context window (the chunk of text it can have in front of it at once), and it has a fixed maximum size. As long as something fits in there, it has it and uses it. Once it stops fitting, as far as it's concerned it doesn't exist: no warning, no recycle bin, no way to get it back. And yes, its own answers also go inside the envelope, and they're usually what takes up the most room: you write three lines and it hands you back sixty.
theory.analogy: Imagine every message of yours is handled by a different intern, freshly arrived, who's handed the complete file to read in two minutes before answering you. If the file doesn't fit in the folder, someone quietly pulls pages off the front without telling them. The intern answers just as confidently, with whatever pages are left.
theory.example: In Marta's message 141, the AI reread all 140 previous ones in full before writing a single word. That's why it took 40 seconds to start when on day one it took 4.

theory.title: Tokens: the unit that measures the room it takes up
theory.text: Text isn't measured in words but in tokens (word chunks). In English, each word usually breaks into one or two tokens: count 1,000 words ≈ 1,300 tokens and you won't be far off. The big apps of 2026 handle windows of 200,000 to 1,000,000 tokens, roughly 150,000 to 750,000 words: somewhere between one fat novel and seven. It sounds infinite, and it isn't, because some things take up far more than they look. A screenshot eats about 1,500 tokens, the same as a thousand words, and a 40-page PDF is about 30,000. A web search it runs on its own drops entire pages you never even saw into the envelope. And your custom instructions and memory silently attach themselves to the start of every chat too, also taking up room. Before your table fills up from talking, it fills up from pasting.
theory.example: Javier, an accountant, pasted his industry's 60-page collective bargaining agreement to ask about overtime. That was about 45,000 tokens in one go. Then he spent 50 messages asking things, and in every one of those 50 messages the whole agreement traveled back inside the envelope again.

theory.title: Forgetting doesn't arrive all at once: it gets dull first
theory.text: Almost nobody ever fully fills the window, and yet everyone experiences this. The reason is quality drops long before memory runs out. When the envelope gets very fat, it reads the beginning and the end well, but skims the middle. That's usually where your important decisions live: you made them in message 30 of 120. The signs are always the same and are worth knowing by heart: it repeats itself, proposes something you'd already ruled out, revives a section you asked to delete, skips the format you requested, goes back to being formal when you told it not to, or starts slipping in phrases in another language. When you see two of those signs in a row, don't argue with it or scold it: the table is saturated. And no, they haven't secretly swapped your model for a worse one, which is what everyone thinks the first time.
theory.analogy: It's a coworker you've been piling papers on top of for six hours. They're still just as good. But now they have to dig through eighty pages every time they open their mouth, and sometimes they grab the wrong one.
theory.example: The sign Marta saw and couldn't read: in message 96, the AI called a section "Workshops" again after they'd been calling it "Classes" since message 40. That was the moment to move. She held on for forty more messages.

theory.title: What a mile-long chat really costs you
theory.text: Since everything gets resent every turn, a long conversation is expensive in three different currencies. The first is time: the fatter the envelope, the longer it takes to start writing, and going from 4 seconds to 40 in the same afternoon is normal. The second is your available messages: on the free plan you run out of the good models much sooner if you're dragging along a huge chat, and on paid plans, which run $20 to $25 a month depending on the app, the exact same thing happens, just later. The third is quality, which is the one that hurts: you pay more and wait longer to get a worse answer than a clean chat would have given you. Slowness is your free tell. When you notice it's taking three times as long as this morning, it's not that the app is having a bad day: it's that you're carrying half a pound of conversation.
theory.example: A 300-message chat with two PDFs pasted in can carry about 120,000 tokens every turn. A freshly opened chat with your project card, about 600. Each answer costs you two hundred times more and isn't two hundred times better.

theory.title: Context isn't memory: the table and the filing cabinet
theory.text: These two get confused all the time and are different things. Context is the table: what it has in front of it right now, fills up and empties out when you close the chat. Memory is notes saved in a separate filing cabinet that the app pastes back on the table at the start of every conversation. That's why it sometimes feels like it knows you: it doesn't remember you, it gets handed the cheat sheet. Projects (a folder of chats with shared instructions and files) and custom instructions do the same thing: they're automatic cheat sheets. All of that is fine, but none of the three is really yours, because it lives inside the app and depends on it. What is truly yours is a text file on your computer with your project's state, which you paste whenever you feel like it, into whichever app you feel like. Warning: deleting the app's memory is irreversible, no undo, no recycle bin, same as deleting a conversation.
theory.analogy: The table gets cleared every night. The filing cabinet stays. But the filing cabinet belongs to the company, not you: you keep your real copy in your own folder.

theory.title: Trim, handoff, and anchor: what to do once it's already gotten messy
theory.text: Three moves and you're more than covered. The first is trimming: when its last answer is bad, don't reply "no, not like that," because that adds two more pages to the pile, the good one and the bad one. Edit your previous message and resend it: the bad answer disappears from the envelope instead of sitting there in the way. The second is the handoff: you ask it for a summary of the conversation written for someone who wasn't there, open a new chat, and paste it as the first message. It sounds like you're going to lose work, and it's the opposite, because the summary keeps the decisions and drops the forty back-and-forths it took to reach them. The third is anchoring: whatever can't afford to fail gets repeated in your last message, because the end of the envelope always gets read well. And above all three, one rule: one chat per topic. Conversations don't die from a single failure, they die from buildup.
theory.example: Marta's handoff ran 40 lines and summarized 140 messages. She pasted it into a new chat and by the second message the green button was already set correctly. Twelve minutes, counting the time it took her to read the summary and correct two things.

tasks.title: Measure how much room a text of yours actually takes up
tasks.action: Open that address. You'll see a big empty text box. Take something real of yours — a long email you sent this week, a page of your notes, your idea's description — and paste it in. Right below the box, two numbers appear: "Tokens" and "Characters." The first is what it takes up on the AI's table. Now do the math: divide the tokens by your text's word count and you'll get something between 1.2 and 1.4. That's the English multiplier and it works for everything else too.
tasks.expect: Two numbers below the box. For an English text of about 500 words you should see between 600 and 700 tokens. Paste 10,000 words and you'll see about 13,000 tokens: that's about 6-7% of a 200,000 window, just from one document.
tasks.stuck: If the page asks for an account or won't load, no problem: multiply your word count by 1.3 and you have the estimate. To count words, in Word it's under "Review" then "Word Count"; in Google Docs, under "Tools" then "Word count."

tasks.title: Give it a trap rule and watch when it stops following it
tasks.where: In the app you use (ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini), in a new chat
tasks.action: Open a new chat, paste the prompt (the message you write to it) below exactly as-is, and wait for its confirmation. From there, put it to work on anything else: ask for twenty long answers in a row, summaries, ideas, recipes, whatever, the longer the better. You only watch one thing: whether the last line keeps showing up. Don't remind it, don't scold it. Just watch.
tasks.prompt: Permanent rule for this whole conversation: end every one of your answers with a final line that says exactly LIVE RULE 🥝. Nothing else, no commentary, no explanation. This is an experiment about your conversation memory, so don't warn me if you notice yourself forgetting: just keep answering normally. Confirm you understood and from there we'll talk about other things.
tasks.expect: The first ten or fifteen answers carry the line. At some point it disappears, or shows up sometimes and not others. That hesitation is exactly what happens with your project decisions, except with the kiwi emoji you can see it and with decisions you can't.
tasks.stuck: If it holds for twenty messages without failing, your app has a big window and your messages are short. Paste three very long texts in a row (whole chapters, meeting minutes, whatever you have on hand) and check again. You can also try uploading four or five screenshots: images fill the table at a surprising rate.

tasks.title: Audit what it still actually has in front of it
tasks.where: In the app, inside one of your conversations that's already long
tasks.action: Go to a real chat, one you've been working in for a while where decisions were made. Paste the prompt below and compare its answer to what you know you actually said. Don't look for it to get it right: look for the gaps.
tasks.prompt:
Stop for a moment before answering anything new. Give me an inventory of what you currently have in front of you in this conversation, in four blocks:
1) Permanent instructions I gave you that you still see written. Quote the literal sentence for each.
2) Decisions that are already settled and not up for discussion.
3) Things we ruled out, and why we ruled them out.
4) Exactly where we left off.
Rule you can't skip: if something isn't literally written earlier in this conversation, write I DON'T HAVE IT instead of reconstructing it from memory. I'd rather have an inventory with gaps than a made-up one. Don't guess and don't fill in blanks.
tasks.expect: A list in four blocks. What's interesting is the absences: if a decision you clearly remember making is missing, or if it misquotes one of your instructions, the table is saturated and it's time to move. If it gets everything right and quotes literally, you have runway left.
tasks.stuck: If it gives you everything perfectly but you know something's missing, ask directly about that specific thing: "search this conversation for where we decided X and quote me the message." If it reconstructs it without being able to quote it, it's making it up, and that's the worst scenario: it looks like it has it and it doesn't.

tasks.title: Write the handoff before you need it
tasks.where: In the app, in that same long conversation
tasks.action: Paste the prompt below. When it gives you the handoff, read the whole thing first, calmly. You'll find two or three things wrong or misreported: fix them yourself by hand right there in the text before using it. That reading time is the task, not a formality.
tasks.prompt:
We're going to move to a new conversation because this one's gotten very long. Write me a handoff document to paste into another AI that hasn't been here and knows nothing. Exact structure:
GOAL: what we're building and for whom, in two sentences.
WHO I AM: my technical level and how I need you to talk to me.
SETTLED DECISIONS: list of things already decided that don't get revisited, one per line.
RULED OUT: what we tried or proposed and dropped, with the reason in half a line.
CURRENT STATE: what's done and working, and what files or pieces already exist.
NEXT STEP: the single thing to do now.
TRAPS: mistakes we've already fallen into in this conversation, so they don't repeat.
Write it in bullet points, no flourishes, don't repeat full code (just file names and what each does). Keep it under 50 lines. If something's unclear, mark it [UNCLEAR] instead of making it up.
tasks.expect: A text of 30 to 50 lines with those seven blocks. Someone coming in cold should be able to read it and know what to do. If you see an [UNCLEAR], that's a good sign: it means it's being honest instead of filling gaps.
tasks.stuck: If it gives you a generic summary like "we talked about your website and various options," tell it: "this doesn't work, it doesn't carry a single concrete decision. Rewrite it with names, numbers, and exact decisions, as they appear in this conversation." Usually one more ask is enough.

tasks.title: Start a new chat and check the handoff works
tasks.where: In the app, "New chat" button, top of the left sidebar
tasks.action: Copy the corrected handoff. Click "New chat." Paste it as the first message, and below the handoff, in that same message, add the prompt below. Don't close or delete the old chat: leave it there. Deleting a conversation is irreversible and someday you'll want to look back at it.
tasks.prompt: That's the handoff from the previous conversation. Before continuing and before writing anything work-related: tell me in three lines what we're building and what the next step is, in your own words. And if anything in the handoff is ambiguous or you're missing information to continue, ask me now. I'd rather answer three questions than discover in half an hour that you understood something else.
tasks.expect: A three-line summary of its own that you recognize as your project, and maybe two or three questions. If it asks something, answer it and add that answer to your saved handoff: you've just found a hole.
tasks.stuck: If the summary it gives back doesn't resemble your project, the handoff is badly written, not the AI. Go back to the old chat, ask again pointing out what failed, and repeat. If the old chat is already so saturated it can't even do that well, write the handoff yourself by hand: twenty lines of yours beat fifty of its.

tasks.title: Trim: edit your message instead of insisting
tasks.where: In the app, over one of your own messages
tasks.action: Find a message of yours that got a bad answer. Hover your mouse over your message (on mobile, press and hold): small icons appear, one shaped like a pencil. Click the pencil, fix your message to ask better, and hit "Send" or "Save and submit." The conversation rebuilds from there: the bad answer is no longer on the table. Notice the small arrows < 1/2 > that appear below the message: they let you move between the two versions. Use this every time the answer is entirely bad. Insisting underneath it leaves the trash inside the envelope forever.
tasks.expect: Your changed message and a new answer right below it. Everything that came after has vanished from view and stopped taking up room. The arrows let you go back to the previous version if you change your mind.
tasks.stuck: If you don't see the pencil, try clicking directly on your message, or widen the browser window: on narrow screens the icons hide. In Gemini the icon is to the right of your message and in some versions it's called "Edit text." If your app doesn't allow editing, the alternative works just as well: copy the handoff and open a new chat.

tasks.title: Anchor what can't afford to fail in your last message
tasks.where: In the app, in any conversation already past thirty messages
tasks.action: Take the three or four rules for your project that would wreck your work if forgotten. For example: "the text goes in plain English," "don't touch the styles file," "no new libraries," "always give me the whole file, not fragments." Paste them at the end of your request, in a separate block, every time you ask for something important. It's not overkill: it's taking advantage of the fact that the end of the envelope always gets read well.
tasks.prompt:
[Write here what you want it to do now]

---
REMINDER OF FIXED RULES (still in effect, even if they haven't come up in a while):
1. All visible text in plain English.
2. Don't modify anything I haven't explicitly asked for.
3. Give me the complete file, not loose fragments with ellipses.
4. If anything I ask for conflicts with a decision we already made, stop and ask me before doing it.
tasks.expect: Answers that stop breaking your rules, even in long chats. You'll especially notice point 4: it starts flagging contradictions instead of plowing ahead and breaking something.
tasks.stuck: If it still breaks the rules, the conversation needs moving, not insisting. Do the handoff and continue in a new chat with this same block in place from the first message.

tasks.title: Build your STATE.txt file outside the AI
tasks.where: In Windows Notepad, Mac TextEdit, or your phone's notes
tasks.action: Create a text file and call it STATE.txt. Save it in your project folder, not on the desktop among forty other things. That's where the short, true version of your project will live: goal, settled decisions, what was ruled out, where you are, and the next step. At the end of every work session, ask the AI for the block below, paste it into the file, and replace what was there. Five minutes a day. This file is the only place your project is truly safe: apps expire, change prices, get their memory wiped, and this file doesn't.
tasks.prompt:
We're done for today. Write me the state block to paste into my STATE.txt file, in exactly this shape and nothing else:
DATE:
GOAL (2 sentences):
SETTLED DECISIONS (bullets):
RULED OUT AND WHY (bullets):
DONE SO FAR (bullets):
NEXT STEP (one line only):
STILL TO DECIDE (bullets):
Plain text, no bold or decorative headers, so I can paste it into Notepad. Above all, don't make up anything we haven't discussed today: if a section is empty, write "none."
tasks.expect: A plain text block you copy as-is. The next day you open a new chat, paste the file, and continue as if nothing happened. It's the same handoff trick, turned into a daily habit.
tasks.stuck: If it comes back with bold, asterisks, and hashtags, don't worry: paste it anyway, it reads fine. If keeping it up feels like too much, at least keep the NEXT STEP line: it's the one that saves the most time when you come back after three days.

tasks.title: Hang your cheat sheet in a Project so you never paste it again
tasks.where: In the app's left sidebar: "Projects" in ChatGPT, "Projects" in Claude, "Gems" in Gemini
tasks.action: In ChatGPT, click "Projects" in the left menu, then the plus sign or "New project"; name your project and inside look for "Instructions" and "Files." In Claude, click "Projects," then "Create project," and inside you'll see "Project knowledge" for uploading files and a box for instructions. In Gemini, look for "Gems" or "Explore Gems" then "New Gem." In any of the three: paste your STATE.txt as a file and write your level and your fixed rules in the instructions box. From then on, every chat you open inside that folder is already born knowing what it's all about.
tasks.expect: A named folder in the sidebar. When you open a chat inside it and ask "what are we building?", it answers without you having pasted anything into that chat.
tasks.stuck: If the option doesn't show up, your plan doesn't include it: Projects usually require the paid plan, $20 to $25 a month depending on the app. It's not required for any part of this course. Pasting your STATE.txt by hand at the start of every chat achieves exactly the same thing and costs you ten seconds.

matters: Its own answers take up more room than your questions. If you ask it to elaborate, give you the entire code every time, or produce mile-long tables, you write three lines and it fills the table. Ignoring this means wondering why it's getting dull when "you've barely written anything."

Degradation warns before it fails. Repeating itself, reviving something ruled out, skipping the format, or slipping back into another language are signs, not quirks. Whoever doesn't read them spends hours arguing with an AI that no longer has what it's arguing about in front of it.

The handoff gets written while the conversation is still going well, not after it's already a mess. A saturated conversation also summarizes badly, and then you move with a summary that left out half your decisions.

What can't afford to fail goes at the start or end of the envelope, never buried in message 40 of 120. It's the difference between it respecting your rules and following them only sometimes without you knowing why.
ignore: The exact number of tokens your app can hold. It changes every few months and you won't make any different decision by knowing it. Watching for slowness and dullness signs is enough.

Counting tokens by hand or keeping a spending spreadsheet. That makes sense when coding against the API (the technical way of connecting to the AI without going through the app), and you're going to work inside the app, where you pay a flat fee.

Long-term memory techniques with external tools: document databases, semantic search, agents with their own memory. They solve a problem you don't have yet. Your twenty-line STATE.txt covers 95% of the ground.
canDo: Summarize its own conversation into a usable handoff, if you give it the structure and forbid it from filling gaps.
Give you an inventory of what it still has in front of it, with literal quotes, when you ask explicitly and allow it to say something isn't there.
Work with long documents if you feed them in chunks with a clear goal per chunk, instead of dumping 300 pages and a vague question.
Rebuild your project's full state in a freshly opened chat from twenty lines of yours, and be producing like yesterday within two messages.
cantDo: Warn you on its own that it's running out of room. Some apps show a notice when the conversation gets very long, but most say nothing: it dulls silently.

Recover what already fell off the table. There's no "look further up" that helps: if it left the envelope, as far as it's concerned it never existed. The only place it still exists is on your screen, and that's where you have to go.

Read a full 300-page PDF and answer precisely about page 187. Often the app doesn't feed it the whole document, just the chunks it deems relevant, and neither it nor you can see which ones got left out.

Honestly tell you "I don't have this in front of me anymore." Its instinct is to reconstruct it with whatever sounds right, and it tells you with the same confidence as when it actually has it. That's why the inventory needs to be requested with the explicit order to write I DON'T HAVE IT.
words: Context window
The chunk of text the AI can have in front of it while answering you. It has a maximum size. Whatever doesn't fit, as far as it's concerned, doesn't exist.
Token
The small chunk text gets split into to measure it. In English, each word gives about one token. Everything that takes up room is counted this way.
Turn
One of your messages plus its answer. Every turn, the whole conversation gets resent from the start.
Handoff
The summary you ask the AI for to paste into a new conversation. It captures decisions and state, and drops the whole path taken to get there.
Trim
Editing a previous message of yours and resending it, instead of continuing to write below it. Whatever came after stops taking up room.
Anchor
Repeating the rules that can't fail at the end of your message, because the end is the part that always gets read well.
Memory
Notes about you the app stores separately and pastes back at the start of every conversation. It feels like it remembers you; really it's handed the cheat sheet. Deleting it can't be undone.
Project (or Gem)
A folder of conversations with shared instructions and files. Anything you open inside it is born already knowing what you've attached to it.
Custom instructions
A fixed text you write once in settings that applies to all your chats: who you are, how you want it to talk to you, what it shouldn't do.
Usage limit
The cap on messages you're allowed to send in a stretch of time. Very long chats burn through it much faster, because every answer requires rereading everything before it.
